summary: Metolazone is a quinazoline thiazide-like diuretic that inhibits sodium reabsorption at the cortical diluting segment (and proximal tubule), producing diuresis and natriuresis used for edema of heart failure and renal disease and for hypertension. Unlike thiazides it retains efficacy at low glomerular filtration rates and is often added to a loop diuretic for synergistic (sequential nephron blockade) diuresis. Key hazards are hypokalemia and other electrolyte/volume disturbances.
indications: Edema of renal disease including nephrotic syndrome and states of diminished renal function
Hypertension, alone or combined with other antihypertensive classes
Off-label: adjunct to loop diuretics for diuretic-resistant edema (sequential nephron blockade)

dosage.n: Begin at lowest dose; allow 3-4 weeks for full effect

dosage.d: 2.5-10 mg given 30 min before a loop diuretic
dosage.n: Risk of profound diuresis and hypokalemia; monitor closely
Risk of precipitating hepatic coma or worsening renal failure

admin: Give a single daily dose, preferably in the morning to limit night-time urination
May be taken with or without food
When combined with a loop diuretic, give metolazone about 30 minutes before the loop agent
Titrate to the minimal dose that maintains the desired response and reduce when the goal is reached
Correct any pre-existing hypokalemia before use in digitalized patients
moa: Metolazone inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption primarily at the cortical diluting segment of the distal convoluted tubule and to a lesser extent at the proximal tubule, increasing distal sodium delivery and thereby potassium excretion. It does not inhibit carbonic anhydrase. By acting at a different nephron site than loop diuretics it produces synergistic (sequential nephron blockade) natriuresis, and unlike most thiazides it remains effective at low glomerular filtration rates.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to metolazone or sulfonamide-derived diuretics
relative: Pre-existing hypokalemia or severe electrolyte imbalance
monitor: Concomitant other antihypertensives or loop diuretics

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; metolazone crosses the placenta. Routine diuretic use in otherwise healthy pregnant women is inappropriate. Use only if clearly needed for pathologic edema, weighing benefit against fetal/neonatal hazards including jaundice and thrombocytopenia.
lact: Metolazone appears in breast milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother.
renal: Retains diuretic efficacy in moderate-to-severe renal impairment, unlike most thiazides, and is useful when GFR is low. Contraindicated in anuria. Monitor electrolytes and renal function closely as azotemia and volume depletion may worsen function.
hepatic: Contraindicated in hepatic coma or precoma. In cirrhosis, electrolyte shifts (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, alkalosis) can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy; use cautiously with close monitoring.

major: Lithium - reduces renal clearance of lithium and adds high risk of lithium toxicity; generally avoid combination
Digitalis glycosides - diuretic-induced hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia increases risk of dangerous arrhythmias
Other loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) - profound additive diuresis with severe fluid/electrolyte loss
moderate: ACE inhibitors / ARBs - additive hypotension and first-dose hypotension; risk of azotemia
Corticosteroids / ACTH - intensified electrolyte depletion, especially hypokalemia
Antidiabetic agents - may reduce glucose control and require dose adjustment
minor: NSAIDs - may blunt the diuretic and antihypertensive response
Curare-type muscle relaxants - effect may be enhanced by hypokalemia
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no significant food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may potentiate orthostatic hypotension; avoid excess.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum uric acid, glucose, calcium and cholesterol and lower serum potassium and sodium; can interfere with parathyroid function tests.

serious: Excessive volume depletion and prerenal azotemia

monitoring: Serum potassium, sodium and other electrolytes at baseline and regularly
Renal function (BUN, creatinine) and fluid/volume status
Serum uric acid and blood glucose periodically
Blood pressure and signs of orthostatic hypotension
Signs of hepatic decompensation in cirrhotic patients
counsel: Take in the morning to avoid waking at night to urinate
Report muscle weakness, cramps, palpitations, severe dizziness or confusion (low potassium/sodium)
Rise slowly from sitting or lying to reduce dizziness
Keep follow-up appointments for blood tests of electrolytes and kidney function
Tell your doctor about lithium, digoxin, blood-pressure or diabetes medicines
pk: Peak diuretic effect within about 2 hours
Store at 20-25 C; protect from light in a tight, light-resistant container
pearls: Unlike standard thiazides, metolazone keeps working at low GFR, making it valuable in renal impairment and refractory edema
Classic use is add-on to a loop diuretic for sequential nephron blockade in diuretic-resistant heart failure - watch for brisk diuresis and hypokalemia
Different oral formulations differ in bioavailability (e.g. Zaroxolyn vs Mykrox); they are not mg-for-mg interchangeable and require dose titration
Hypokalemia is dose-related and especially dangerous in digitalized patients - monitor and supplement potassium
Sulfonamide-derived; use caution in patients with known sulfonamide hypersensitivity
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember the same day; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your usual once-daily schedule. Do not double the dose. Avoid taking late in the day to prevent night-time urination.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive diuresis with dehydration, hypotension, electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), lethargy and possibly cardiac arrhythmias or coma. There is no specific antidote. Treat with fluid and electrolyte replacement, supportive care and monitoring of vital signs, electrolytes and renal function; manage symptomatic hypotension and arrhythmias.
